analysis.one_liner: Toughens Clean Water Act enforcement with minimum fines, mandatory inspections, and a polluter-funded enforcement trust fund.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 23 cosponsors, including 4 Republicans, but was referred to a House subcommittee on October 10, 1991, and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would crack down on factories and sewage plants that violate their water pollution permits. It would force penalties to be at least as large as the money a violator saved by polluting, set minimum fines for serious and repeat violations, require regular inspections with independent lab testing, let citizens sue over past violations, and create a trust fund paid for with polluters' penalties to finance inspections and enforcement.
analysis.who_benefits: People who swim in, fish from, drink, or live downstream of polluted water. The bill's own findings said permit violators often faced penalties smaller than the money they saved by polluting, and that lawful facilities were penalized by having to compete with lawbreakers. Higher minimum fines, mandatory inspections with independent lab sampling, an annual public list of repeat violators, expanded citizen suits (including for downstream water users), and a penalty-funded enforcement trust fund would all work to make polluting stop being the cheaper option. Communities near violators would also gain the right to prompt written notice — within two hours — of dangerous discharges.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities and water users downstream of polluters

how_it_helps.text: Requires civil penalties to be no less than the economic benefit or savings a violator gained from polluting, plus interest, closing the gap where breaking the permit rules was cheaper than complying.

Sets minimum penalties of $1,000 for a first serious discharge violation and $5,000 for repeat violations or for 'significant noncompliers,' who would also face mandatory EPA inspections and an annual public list published in the Federal Register and sent to Congress and state governors.

Requires at least annual independent sampling of effluent from major industrial and municipal dischargers — tested by a lab not owned or managed by the permittee — plus monthly discharge reports from major dischargers and written notice to EPA within 2 hours of a discharge likely to endanger health or the environment.
Expands citizen lawsuits to cover past violations of pollution limits and lets downstream water users sue, and allows courts to direct civil penalties toward environmental mitigation projects.

Creates a Clean Water Trust Fund out of the penalties collected, which the EPA Administrator would use to pay for inspections and enforcement, and raises the ceiling on administrative penalties to $25,000 per violation per day.

analysis.who_pays: Industrial facilities and municipal sewage plants that discharge pollutants into water, and the significant industrial users piping waste into sewage treatment plants. They would face minimum and larger penalties tied to the economic benefit of violating, at least annual inspections with independent lab testing, monthly monitoring reports signed by a top facility official, permit requirements for industrial users of sewage plants, and no ability to compromise penalties below set floors. Some costs at municipal treatment plants would likely flow to local ratepayers.

drawbacks.text: Publicly owned sewage treatment plants would take on new federal duties: requiring monthly discharge reports from significant industrial users, permitting them, and — within three years — being granted state authority to inspect and penalize those users. Those compliance costs would partly land on municipal utilities and their ratepayers.

The bill shifts power from states to Washington: it removes provisions allowing a state enforcement action to bar a duplicate federal enforcement action and bars the adequacy of federal-state consultation from being used as a defense in penalty proceedings, leaving states less room to run enforcement their own way.

The minimum penalties apply regardless of a violator's size or ability to pay — $1,000 for a first serious exceedance and $5,000 per repeat violation within 180 days — and the bill forbids compromising penalties for serious violators, which could bear heavily on small operators.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core fix — making penalties at least as large as the money saved by polluting — targets a problem the bill's own findings documented: violations dragged on for long periods, penalties were often smaller than the violator's gain, and law-abiding facilities paid the price of competing against violators. Most costs fall on violators, which is the point. The honest costs are the new monitoring and reporting burdens on municipal sewage plants (partly passed to ratepayers) and a real transfer of enforcement discretion from states to EPA. On balance the benefits to public health and clean water outweigh those costs, though the one-size minimum fines are a blunt instrument for small operators.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in a House subcommittee — referred to the Water Resources Subcommittee on October 10, 1991 — and the committee never brought it up before the Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone introduced the bill on September 26, 1991, and it was referred to the House Committee on Public Works and Transportation.
On October 10, 1991, it was referred to the committee's Subcommittee on Water Resources, which was the last action ever taken on it.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote followed, and the bill died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Facilities that were violating their water pollution permits came out ahead: the status quo the bill described — penalties often smaller than the economic benefit of polluting, with slow and ineffective enforcement — stayed in place for another Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Water polluters who faced only weak penalties

against.name: House Public Works and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after its September 26, 1991 referral, passed it to the Water Resources Subcommittee on October 10, and never reported it for a House vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a floor vote, so there were no roll calls; sponsorship was mostly Democratic (19 of 23 cosponsors) but included 4 Republicans.

industries.industry: Industrial polluters (permitted factory and plant dischargers)
industries.note: The bill's whole purpose is to make violation stop paying: minimum and uncompromisable penalties, fines at least equal to the economic benefit of polluting, mandatory inspections with independent lab testing, monthly reporting, and an annual public list of significant noncompliers. Its interest runs directly against the public's interest in clean water.

Plants would face federal enforcement of pretreatment rules, permit-level annual inspections, and the duty to police their industrial users. But they would also gain state-granted authority to inspect and fine the industries dumping into their systems — a tool many currently lack.

industries.industry: Industrial users of municipal sewage treatment plants
industries.note: Significant industrial users piping waste into sewage plants would have to hold a permit, file monthly discharge monitoring reports as a condition of using the plant, and face federal, state, and plant-level penalties for violating pretreatment limits.

industries.industry: Environmental testing labs and inspection services
industries.note: Mandatory annual sampling of major dischargers, analyzed by federal, state, or approved independent laboratories, plus a penalty-funded inspection program, would expand demand for independent water testing and inspection work.
